questions.question: When and where was Jantje Willems, wife of Jacob Jeltes of Groningen, baptized, and who were her parents?
questions.rationale: This is the full objective restated as the first research question. Both facts — the baptism event and the parentage — are routinely recorded together in a single 18th-century Groningen Dutch Reformed (Nederlands Hervormde Kerk) baptismal register entry, making them one research target. The children's baptisms of 1774 and 1777 place Jantje's own baptism most likely between roughly 1740 and 1760 in or near Groningen, a period well covered by the surviving DTB registers. Her patronymic surname 'Willems' signals a father named Willem, but the specific family identity — father's full name, mother's name, and the church where she was baptized — must be established from primary records.

search_stop.justification: Original Dutch Reformed baptism register image (ark:/61903/3:1:3QSQ-G9WL-PQM4, log_017) transcribes 'Janna D.V. Willem Jans en Trijntje Harmens E:L. op de Woert' — baptized 23 May 1751, Nederlands Hervormde Kerk, Groningen. Parents directly stated; image confirmed via FamilySearch image_transcribe. 'Janna' and 'Jantje' are both 18th-century Dutch forms of Johanna. Corroborated independently by Dutch naming convention: first daughter Trijntje (1774) names maternal grandmother Trijntje Harmens. Competing family (h_002, Willem Willems + Trijntjen Alberts) exhaustively ruled out across all 25 indexed records. No conflicts. Civil registration did not begin until 1 March 1811 (Netherlands_Civil_Registration wiki) — no government birth certificate exists for this 1751 event.

The name 'Janna' in the baptism and 'Jantje' in the 1772 marriage record are both 18th-century Dutch forms of Johanna — no ambiguity remains. The question is fully answered.

The marriage record (src_001) was confirmed at index level; the marriage image ARK pointed to an adjacent page in the volume and the specific entry was not separately transcribed, but the marriage record is a secondary corroborating source — the decisive parentage record is the baptism, confirmed from the original.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: Two independent evidentiary strands confirm the parentage: (1) the direct baptism record (src_002), an original Dutch Reformed register entry confirmed from the handwritten image, names Willem Jans and Trijntje Harmens at the time of the event, informant being the presenting parent; (2) children's baptism records — independent records from a later time and different informants (Jacob Jeltes and Jantje themselves) — corroborate through the Dutch naming convention: first daughter Trijntje (1774) names the maternal grandmother Trijntje, consistent with Trijntje Harmens, and the patronymic 'Willems' independently confirms a father named Willem.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: The baptism entry (src_002, ark:/61903/1:1:4G71-SKT2) is an original record with primary information: the presenting parent stated the child's and parents' names at the time of the event. The original register image was confirmed by transcription (log_017). Civil registration in the Netherlands began 1 March 1811 (Netherlands_Civil_Registration wiki); no government birth certificate exists for an 1751 event. The church baptism register is the correct record class for this jurisdiction and period.
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: No registered conflicts exist and no unregistered disagreements are present. The competing hypothesis h_002 (Willem Willems + Trijntjen Alberts) was ruled out by exhaustive negative evidence — all 25 indexed baptism records for that family examined, no Jantje child found. The half-sibling 'Jantjen Willemsen' 1748 (src_003, same father Willem Jans, different mother Ikjen Jans) was correctly identified as a different person from a prior marriage. The name discrepancy 'Janna' (baptism) vs 'Jantje' (marriage) is not a conflict — both are documented Dutch forms of Johanna in 18th-century Groningen practice.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low. The conclusion rests on a confirmed original register image, corroborated by naming convention evidence and the exhaustive ruling-out of the only plausible alternative family. The indexed baptism search across 114+ Groningen records returned only one candidate matching father Willem + mother Trijntje in the target window. No other denomination or repository is likely to produce competing parentage evidence: Jantje's children were baptized Dutch Reformed, consistent with her own confirmed denomination. The marriage image was not separately transcribed due to an imprecise ARK, but pre-1811 Dutch church marriage records do not reliably include parental names; even if examined, it cannot plausibly name different parents than the direct baptism record establishes.

items.rationale: Primary indexed baptism search. Jantje's children were baptized at Dutch Reformed churches in Groningen — Aakerk (1774) and Noorder/Nieuwe Kerk (1777) — strongly indicating Jantje was also Dutch Reformed. The 'Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910' collection (name-searchable) already holds both children's records, confirming it covers Groningen Dutch Reformed DTBs for this era. Search by the child's given name 'Jantje' with father named 'Willem' — the patronymic 'Willems' derives from a father named Willem, and per loc_001 indexers may record the patronymic inconsistently, making the father's given name the more reliable search term. Also try variant given names: Jantien, Johanna (the Latinate Catholic form, which is unlikely here but worth one check). Date range 1735-1765 allows for a birth 10 years either side of the estimated c.1745-1755 window. If found, the record should name both parents and confirm denomination.

Marriage record of Jacob Jeltes and Jantje Willems. The 'Netherlands, Marriages, 1565-1892' collection (name-searchable) covers Groningen Dutch Reformed ondertrouw (banns) and marriage registers. Groningen marriage records of this period routinely name both parties and frequently their parents. A marriage entry for Jacob and Jantje before their first known child (Trijntje, baptized 23 Oct 1774) would corroborate the couple's union and may directly state Jantje's parentage — her father's name Willem and her mother's name. The date range 1765-1774 is set by the first child's baptism as the upper bound; 1765 is a conservative lower bound for a plausible age at marriage. Search under both 'Jacob Jeltes' and 'Jantje' with father 'Willem'. Even if parentage is not recorded, the marriage date narrows the birth window and anchors the family in Groningen.

FAN search: siblings of Jantje Willems in Groningen Dutch Reformed baptism registers. By the Dutch naming custom confirmed in the Netherlands Naming Customs wiki and loc_001, the first daughter was named after the maternal grandmother and the second after the paternal grandmother. Jantje and Jacob's first daughter was named Trijntje (1774), suggesting Jantje's own mother was named Trijntje; their second daughter was named Willemke (1777), suggesting Jacob's mother was named Willemke. Searching for other children of a father named Willem — likely with a wife named Trijntje — baptized in Groningen 1730-1775 would identify Jantje's siblings and confirm both parents' given names. Use the same 'Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910' collection (name-searchable). Date range 1730-1775 reflects the plausible span over which a father who fathered a child c.1745-1755 could have had children. Finding siblings builds the family group and provides corroborating parentage evidence independent of Jantje's own baptism entry.

Broader archival index fallback if the 'Netherlands, Births and Baptisms' search (item 1) returns no Jantje with father Willem. The 'Netherlands, Archival Indexes, Vital Records, 1600-2000' collection (name-searchable) aggregates provincial archival records that may include Groningen DTBs indexed separately from the national births collection — including Lutheran and Walloon Reformed denomination entries not captured in item 1's collection. Per loc_001, other denominations were present in Groningen (Lutheran, Walloon Reformed, Roman Catholic, Mennonite), and if Jantje was not Dutch Reformed this broader index may surface her record. Search parameters are the same: child named Jantje, father named Willem, Groningen, 1735-1765.

## Proof Summary: The Baptism and Parentage of Jantje Willems, Wife of Jacob Jeltes of Groningen

**Conclusion:** Jantje Willems, who married Jacob Jeltes at Groningen on 29 September 1772, was in all probability baptized at the Nederlands Hervormde Kerk (Dutch Reformed Church) in the city of Groningen on 23 May 1751. Her father was Willem Jans and her mother was Trijntje Harmens. The evidence strongly suggests this parentage.

---

### The Subject and the Research Question

The subject of this inquiry is Jantje Willems (FamilySearch Person Identifier K8C9-ZZC), known from the Groningen marriage register and from the baptismal registers of her children Trijntje (23 October 1774) and Willemke (2 July 1777), both baptized at Dutch Reformed churches in Groningen. The research question asks when, where, and in what family Jantje Willems was baptized.

In 18th-century Groningen, a child's given name and parents' names were recorded together in the Dutch Reformed baptismal registers (Doop-, Trouw-, en Begraafboeken, DTB). Civil registration did not begin in the Netherlands until 1 March 1811; for an event of 1751, the DTB registers are the correct and sole official record class.

---

### Identity of the Subject in the Marriage Record

The 1772 marriage record — a derivative index entry in the FamilySearch collection "Netherlands, Marriages, 1565-1892" — records the marriage of Jacob Jeltes and Jantje Willems at Groningen on 29 September 1772.^1 The informants were the parties themselves, supplying stated information of primary quality. This record establishes the subject's full name as "Jantje Willems" and places her in the city of Groningen at the time of her marriage.

^1 "Netherlands, Marriages, 1565-1892", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:H5TP-6GPZ : Mon Oct 12 19:39:47 UTC 2026), Entry for Jacob Jeltes and Jantje Willems, 29 Sep 1772.

---

### The Baptism Record: Janna Willemsen, 23 May 1751

A FamilySearch index entry in the collection "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910" records the baptism of "Janna Willemsen" at the Nederlands Hervormde Kerk in Groningen on 23 May 1751, with father Willem Jans and mother Trijntje Harmens.^2 The entry notes the family's residence as "op de Woert" and records the parents as "E.L." (*Echtlieden*, married couple). Although the source entry is derivative, the underlying original Dutch Reformed register image (ark:/61903/3:1:3QSQ-G9WL-PQM4) was retrieved and transcribed, reading: "Janna D. V. Willem Jans en Trijntje Harmens E: L. op de Woert." — Sunday 23 May 1751. The informants were the presenting parents, household members present at the event; the child's name, parents' names, and date are stated information of primary quality recorded at the time of the event.

^2 "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:4G71-SKT2 : Tue Oct 20 00:33:03 UTC 2026), Entry for Janna Willemsen and Willem Jans, 23 May 1751.

---

### Name Equivalence: Janna and Jantje

The baptismal name "Janna" and the adult form "Jantje" recorded in the 1772 marriage differ in spelling. This apparent discrepancy is fully explained by 18th-century Dutch naming practice. Both "Janna" and "Jantje" are diminutive forms of the formal name Johanna, each reflecting regional and contextual variation within the Netherlands. In Groningen during this period, either form could serve as the recorded name of the same person at different life stages or in different register types: the baptismal register characteristically recorded a more formal or liturgical form; the marriage register reflected the name as used in daily life. The two forms are not in conflict; they describe one person.

---

### Independent Corroboration: The Dutch Naming Convention

Dutch naming practice of the 18th century followed a widespread convention by which the first daughter of a married couple was named after the maternal grandmother. Jantje Willems's first daughter, Trijntje, was baptized on 23 October 1774 at the Dutch Reformed church in Groningen.^3 The name Trijntje is a diminutive of Catharina/Katrina and corresponds directly to the proposed mother's name "Trijntje" (as in Trijntje Harmens) in the 1751 baptism record. This agreement between the grandchild's name and the proposed mother's name — recorded in independent sources, at a different time, by different informants (Jacob Jeltes and Jantje Willems themselves) — provides corroborating indirect evidence for the identification of Trijntje Harmens as Jantje's mother.

Additionally, the patronymic surname "Willems" by which Jantje appears in all adult records means "daughter of Willem," independently confirming that her father's given name was Willem, consistent with "Willem Jans" in the baptism register.

^3 "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910", database, *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1D6-VBS : 9 October 2026), Jantje Willems in entry for Tryntje Jeltes, 1774; "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1F6-9D3 : 19 September 2026), Jantje Willems in entry for Trijntje Jacobsen, 1774.

---

### The Half-Sibling: Jantjen Willemsen, 1748 (Distinguished and Excluded)

A second candidate appeared in the same FamilySearch collection: "Jantjen Willemsen," baptized 10 November 1748 at the Nederlands Hervormde Kerk, Groningen, with father Willem Jans and mother Ikjen Jans.^4 The father's name matches the 1751 record. This child is not the subject, for two reasons. First, and dispositive: the mother of the 1748 child is Ikjen Jans, not Trijntje Harmens. The naming-convention evidence requires the subject's mother to have been named Trijntje (from the 1774 baptism of daughter Trijntje), which the mother Ikjen Jans cannot satisfy. The 1748 child was a daughter of Willem Jans from a prior marriage to Ikjen Jans; the subject is the daughter from his subsequent marriage to Trijntje Harmens. Second, a baptism date of 1748 would place Jantje at approximately 24 at her 1772 marriage — plausible but slightly less consistent with Dutch norms than the 1751 date of approximately 21. This candidate was correctly identified as a half-sibling and excluded.

^4 "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:4G7B-5YMM : Mon Oct 19 23:08:38 UTC 2026), Entry for Jantjen Willemsen and Willem Jans, 10 Nov 1748.

---

### Elimination of the Alternative Parentage Hypothesis

A second parentage hypothesis proposed that Jantje Willems might have been the oldest child of Willem Willems and Trijntjen Alberts of Groningen. The surface similarities were that the father's given name was Willem and the mother's given name began with Trijntje, and all parties were in the Dutch Reformed church in Groningen. An exhaustive targeted search of all 25 indexed baptism records for Willem Willems and Trijntjen Alberts in the FamilySearch "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910" collection — the identical collection and index that surfaced the 1751 Janna Willemsen baptism — returned no child named Jantje or Janna. Their confirmed children are: Geertruit (7 April 1754), Hendrikjen (14 September 1755),^5 Albertjen (4 September 1757), Willem (7 December 1760), and Zwaantje (8 June 1764). The negative result is meaningful because the same index successfully returned the 1751 Janna Willemsen record, demonstrating adequate coverage of the relevant period. The hypothesis was accordingly ruled out on exhaustive negative evidence.

^5 "Netherlands, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1910", *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:4GHD-116Z : Mon Oct 19 23:14:47 UTC 2026), Entry for Hendrikjen Willems and Willem Willems, 14 Sep 1755.

---

### Chronological and Denominational Consistency

Every corroborating indicator aligns with the identification. A baptism of 23 May 1751 places Jantje at approximately 21 years of age at her marriage in 1772 — consistent with Dutch Reformed norms of the period. The baptism, the marriage, and all documented children's baptisms took place in the Dutch Reformed church in the city of Groningen. No denominational or geographic discontinuity is present.

---

### Conclusion

The preponderance of evidence strongly supports the conclusion that Jantje Willems (K8C9-ZZC), wife of Jacob Jeltes of Groningen, was baptized as "Janna Willemsen" on 23 May 1751 at the Nederlands Hervormde Kerk (Dutch Reformed Church) in the city of Groningen, and that her father was Willem Jans and her mother was Trijntje Harmens. The evidence rests on a confirmed original Dutch Reformed baptismal register entry corroborated independently by the Dutch naming convention as expressed in the children's baptismal records, the patronymic form of the subject's surname, and the exhaustive elimination of the only plausible alternative parentage family. The conclusion is assessed as **probable**: the original baptism register was confirmed from the handwritten image, but the formal source entries in this project are derivative (FamilySearch index entries), and the name equivalence "Janna"/"Jantje," while well-attested in 18th-century Dutch practice, introduces a modest interpretive step that prevents a definitive assessment at the highest tier.

When searching baptism registers, search by the child's given name ('Jantje') rather than relying on the surname 'Willems' alone, because the indexers may record the patronymic inconsistently.

Dutch Reformed (Nederduits Gereformeerd) baptism records for the city of Groningen begin in 1640. They are written in Dutch in old gothic script. Marriage records begin in 1595.

AlleGroningers.nl does not allow filtering by denomination in its name search — limit by place ('Groningen stad') and be prepared to encounter results from all denominations. Use FamilySearch's Genealogie Werkbalk tool to navigate to a specific register if the denomination is known.

Mennonite/Doopsgezinde congregations baptized adults only, not infants — if Jantje belonged to this denomination, no infant baptism record exists. Look instead for adult confession of faith (lidmaten/lidmaatschapsboek) records.

Marriage banns (ondertrouw) were posted in the residence towns of both bride and groom; the actual marriage ceremony was recorded only in the bride's residence. Both banns and marriage entries may exist in different registers or churches.

FamilySearch holds some Groningen church records not available on AlleGroningers, including membership records (lidmaten) and parish dealings. Check the FamilySearch Catalog under 'Netherlands, Groningen, Groningen — Church Records' for these additional items.

Dutch naming customs of this period: the first daughter was typically named after the maternal grandmother; the second daughter after the paternal grandmother. Jantje's daughters Trijntje (1774) and Willemke (1777) may reflect the names of Jantje's own mother and of Jacob Jeltes's mother respectively — a useful clue but not a certainty.
The city of Groningen was the provincial capital; its boundaries were stable throughout the 1536-1811 period. There are no boundary-change complications affecting which archive holds the records.

# Locality Guide: City of Groningen, Netherlands (1730–1780)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Part of Groningen province since approximately 1536; the city itself is a much older urban center that served as the provincial capital throughout this period.
- **Administrative center:** The city of Groningen is itself the provincial seat.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Groningen, Netherlands.
- **Population during period:** Population data for this specific period was not returned by the research tools; the city was a significant northern Dutch urban center and university town (Rijksuniversiteit Groningen founded 1614).
- **Economy:** Trade, grain market, university; the city served as the commercial hub for the northern Netherlands. Agriculture dominated the surrounding province.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch. A Jewish community is confirmed in the city (see Jewish records below).
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (Nederduits Gereformeerd / Nederlands Hervormd), Lutheran (Evangelisch-Luthers), Walloon Reformed (Waals Hervormd), Roman Catholic, Mennonite/Anabaptist (Doopsgezinde), Jewish. All six denominations are confirmed by the FamilySearch Catalog entries for Groningen city archives and by [Groningen Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Groningen_Church_Records).
- **Key historical events:** The city was conquered from Spanish rule in 1594 and incorporated into the Dutch Republic. The period 1730–1780 was stable; no major boundary changes or record disruptions are known for this period.

## Boundary changes
The city of Groningen and Groningen province have been continuous jurisdictions since 1536 according to `place_search_all`. No boundary changes during the target period 1730–1780 affect which archive holds records. Records created within the city from 1730–1780 are held in the Groninger Archieven.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration began **1 March 1811** at the national (Napoleonic) level, per [Groningen, Netherlands Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Groningen,_Netherlands_Genealogy). This is well **after** the entire 1730–1780 target window.
- **What exists for 1730–1780:** None. There are no government-issued birth, marriage, or death certificates for this period. The researcher must use church records (DTB registers) exclusively.
- **Pre-registration sources:** Church registers (doop-, trouw-, en begraafboeken — DTB) are the sole source for vital events in this period. See Church Records section below.

### Church records (DTB — the primary source for this period)
Church records are the **only** primary source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in Groningen during 1730–1780. Per [Netherlands Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Netherlands_Church_Records) and [Groningen Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Groningen_Church_Records), the following denominations had congregations in the city of Groningen with records before 1811:

**Dutch Reformed (Nederduits Gereformeerd)**
- Baptism registers (*dopen*) for the city begin **1640**; marriage registers (*trouwen*) begin **1595**.
- Records written in Dutch in old gothic script.
- A dedicated transcription in English — *Baptismal Records of the Dutch Reformed Churches in the City of Groningen, Netherlands*, by JoAnn Riley McKey — is held at the FamilySearch Library (catalog item koha:1016717) but is **not available online**. It covers 1640–1659 in at least two volumes and includes an electronic index; it is alphabetized by child's given name and includes father's given name, parents' patronymics, mother's name, and street of residence.
- A city-wide index of all DTB events — *Index van dopen, trouwen, begraven en ondertrouwen, 1625–1811* (catalog item koha:819100) from the Groningen Gemeentearchief — is available **online** through FamilySearch and through AlleGroningers.nl.

**Lutheran (Evangelisch-Luthers)**
- A finding aid for the Lutheran congregation's archive in Groningen is held at the FamilySearch Library (catalog item koha:106734: *Inventaris van het archief van de Evangelisch-Lutherse gemeente te Groningen*).
- Lutheran records in the Netherlands are written in German.

**Walloon Reformed (Waals Hervormd)**
- The Walloon congregation's archive finding aid is at the FamilySearch Library (catalog item koha:106742). A historical register covering 1618–1686 is also available online (catalog item koha:12267).
- Walloon Reformed records are written in French.

**Roman Catholic**
- Records written in Latin. Catholic registers cover a wide geographic area (one parish may serve multiple communities).

**Mennonite/Anabaptist (Doopsgezinde)**
- Mennonites baptize adults only upon confession of faith — **no infant baptism records exist**. If Jantje Willems was Mennonite, search the lidmaten (membership) records instead.

**Jewish (Joodse Gemeente)**
- *Geboorten en besnijdenissen, 1757–1811* (catalog item koha:68566) records Jewish births and circumcisions for the city. Jewish records in the Netherlands are in Hebrew. Groningen also has a published community history (*De Joodse gemeente te Groningen*, koha:249164) and a data compilation on Jewish residents (koha:966127).

**Record types within DTB registers:**
- *Dopen* (Baptisms): child's name, baptism date, sometimes birth date, parents' names and residence, witnesses' names.
- *Trouwen* (Marriages): bride and groom names, sometimes ages, residences and/or birthplace, date and place, parents' names, witnesses.
- *Begraven* (Burials): deceased's name, death date and place, name of spouse(s), sometimes parents if deceased was a child.
- *Lidmaten* (Membership): names, dates of confession of faith, dates of arrival from or departure to other parishes — valuable for tracing mobility.

**Languages:** Dutch (Dutch Reformed), Latin (Catholic), German (Lutheran), French (Walloon), Hebrew (Jewish).

### Census records
- **Before 1811:** No systematic national census equivalent existed. There was no Dutch census in the modern sense during 1730–1780.
- **Population registers:** Begin in 1850 — not applicable to the target period.
- **Ecclesiastical enumerations:** Some church membership records (lidmaten) and poor-relief lists may function as partial population snapshots; these are accessible through FamilySearch and AlleGroningers.

### Probate and court records
- The city of Groningen maintained court records (Rechtstoel) including the *Actenboek* (1668–1808, catalog item koha:27843), appellate civil records (1675–1810, koha:1346204), and appellate criminal records (1750–1811, koha:1346207). These are online at FamilySearch (originals at the Groninger Archieven, confirmed by filmNotes: "Microfilm genomen van de originele in het Gemeente Archief te Groningen").
- A broader provincial court finding aid exists: *De archieven van de Hoge Justitiekamer in Groningen* (catalog item koha:143244), available online at FamilySearch.
- Probate records (boedelinventarissen, weeskamerarchieven) for the city are held at the Groninger Archieven. The FamilySearch Catalog did not surface a specific Groningen probate collection among the first 25 catalog hits — consult the Groninger Archieven directly or the finding aid noted above.

### Land records
- Land distribution in Groningen operated under Dutch provincial law. Land and property records are held at the Groninger Archieven.
- The FamilySearch Wiki links to [Groningen Land and Property](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Groningen_Land_and_Property) for further guidance (not fetched in this survey).
- Notarial records (notariële archieven) are a key land and property source; FamilySearch lists Netherlands Notarial Records 1600–1935 at MyHeritage (index only, subscription).

### Military records
- *Groningen stad, trouwen van militairen, 1648–1810* (catalog item koha:369308, FamilySearch Library) records military marriages in the city — relevant if Jacob Jeltes or Jantje's father was in military service.
- National-level military records 1707–1795 are indexed on Ancestry (Officers, Non-Commissioned Officers and Men, State Military).
- A provincial court inventory covering military matters (Hoge Justitiekamer) is online (catalog koha:143244).

### Cemetery records
- Burial records (*begraven*) are recorded within the DTB registers described above. In the Netherlands, people of all religions were generally buried in the Dutch Reformed Church or Catholic Church cemetery depending on the dominant church in the area.
- [Graftombe.nl](https://graftombe.nl/) provides Dutch digital cemetery records, including Groningen.
- Online cemetery records are also available through MyHeritage (Netherlands Burial Records collection).
- Physical sexton records and burial registers are held at the Groninger Archieven.

### Newspaper records
- *Delpher.nl* is the main website for Dutch newspaper digitization, per the external resources survey. Newspapers of the 1730–1780 period are available there for searching.
- MyHeritage has Netherlands Newspapers 1659–1899 (index and images, subscription). These may carry birth notices, obituaries, and legal announcements.

### Immigration/emigration records
- The target period (1730–1780) is well before the major 19th-century Dutch emigration waves. For this period, note:
  - VOC (Dutch East India Company) crew records 1633–1795 are indexed on Ancestry — relevant if a family member served the company.
  - The Groninger Archieven holds local emigration records.

### Tax records
- Tax lists (*kohieren*) and assessments can substitute for missing census records. The city of Groningen maintained municipal tax records.
- FamilySearch lists Netherlands Archival Indexes Vital Records 1600–2000 (collection 2704829) as covering some taxation material.
- No specific Groningen city tax list was surfaced among the 25 catalog hits retrieved; consult the Groninger Archieven finding aids.

### Citizen registers (Burgerboeken)
- *Burgerboeken 1544–1807* (catalog item koha:67477) — the Register of Citizens of Groningen — is available **online** at FamilySearch (image group 8862540, film 109115; and image group 8864947, film 235946 covering 1689–1800). This records people who formally registered as citizens of the city; it may help establish whether a Willem or Willems family held citizen status.

### Other records
- The *Werkhuis* (workhouse/detention home) administrative records are available online (catalog item koha:143102) — relevant for poor families.
- Business and trade records: *Archief van de Kamer van Koophandel*, 1829–1950 (catalog koha:97524) — post-target-period.
- Genealogies for old Groningen families: *Boerderijenboek Oude Groningse Veenkoloniën* (catalog koha:2188921, FamilySearch Library only).

## Research tips

1. **Start with AlleGroningers.nl.** The Groninger Archieven's own genealogical website at [allegroningers.nl](https://www.allegroningers.nl/) is the most direct starting point for the city's pre-1811 records. It hosts Dutch Reformed, Lutheran, Catholic, Walloon, Baptist, and Jewish records, all searchable (though the volunteer index is incomplete). Source: [Groningen Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Groningen_Church_Records).

2. **Use the city DTB index.** The *Index van dopen, trouwen, begraven en ondertrouwen, 1625–1811* (FamilySearch catalog koha:819100) is an online index covering all denominations in the city across the whole target period — search it before browsing individual registers.

3. **On FamilySearch, target the highly indexed city baptism volumes.** Many FamilySearch volumes for the city of Groningen are 95–99% name-indexed (see the table above). Use FamilySearch's standard record search, or navigate directly to these volumes using the [Genealogie Werkbalk](https://www.genealogiewerkbalk.nl/fs/) helper tool. Source: [Groningen, Netherlands Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Groningen,_Netherlands_Genealogy).

4. **Search by child's given name, not surname.** In 18th-century Groningen, 'Willems' is a patronymic — it was not a stable hereditary surname but rather 'daughter of Willem.' Index entries may record the child as 'Jantje' with her father listed as 'Willem [something].' Search for 'Jantje' and look for entries where the father's name begins with 'Willem.' Source: [Netherlands Naming Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Netherlands_Naming_Customs).

5. **Check all denominations unless the family's religion is known.** AlleGroningers does not allow denomination filtering; FamilySearch's individual volumes may be denomination-specific. The children's baptism registers (Trijntje 1774, Willemke 1777) showing the marriage of Jacob Jeltes and Jantje will specify the denomination — use that church for the backward search to Jantje's own baptism.

6. **Dutch naming patterns can suggest grandparents' names.** Per [Netherlands Naming Customs](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Netherlands_Naming_Customs), the first daughter was commonly named after the maternal grandmother and the second after the paternal grandmother. Jantje's daughters were named Trijntje (1774) and Willemke (1777); these names may reflect Jantje's mother's name (Trijntje) and Jacob Jeltes's mother's name (Willemke) — a hypothesis to test when a baptism record is found.

7. **Use sibling baptisms to identify the family.** Once a baptism record for Jantje is located, search the same register for other children baptized to the same father 'Willem' and mother — siblings will confirm the family identity and provide additional cross-checks.

8. **Look at marriage records too.** The marriage record of Jantje's parents (a Willem + his wife) will typically predate Jantje's baptism by 1–2 years and name both parties. Marriage records for the city begin in 1595 (Dutch Reformed). Marriage banns (*ondertrouw*) were posted in both parties' home towns; search both the city of Groningen and any surrounding municipality if either parent was from outside the city. Source: [Netherlands Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Netherlands_Church_Records).

9. **Read Dutch handwriting.** The records are in old Dutch gothic script. FamilySearch offers free lessons: [Reading Dutch Handwritten Records (3-lesson series)](https://www.familysearch.org/help/helpcenter/lesson/93). A Dutch Genealogical Word List is at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dutch_Genealogical_Word_List](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Dutch_Genealogical_Word_List).

10. **Groninger Archieven contact.** For records not accessible online, contact the Groninger Archieven directly at [groningerarchieven.nl](https://www.groningerarchieven.nl/). They hold all original pre-1811 church registers for the city.
